The one thing that might reverse it is the discovery of a weapon – or, to put it more broadly, of a method of fighting – not dependent on huge concentrations of industrial plant.

…

Had the atomic bomb turned out to be something as cheap and easily manufactured as a bicycle or an alarm clock, it might well have plunged us back into barbarism, but it might, on the other hand, have meant the end of national sovereignty and of the highly-centralised police State. If, as seems to be the case, it is a rare and costly object as difficult to produce as a battleship, it is likelier to put an end to large-scale wars at the cost of prolonging indefinitely a “peace that is no peace”.

Of all the technologies on the horizon, I do worry that freedom and democracy might be especially threatened by a system that could permanently devalue human cognitive labor. My favorite way these arguments are applied to AI is Ben Garfinkel’s work on the relationship between technology and political systems. He has a short blog post summarizing his research on the risks advanced AI poses to democracy here. Here’s the main argument:

Most AI researchers believe that automated systems will eventually be able to perform all of the same tasks that people can. According to one survey, the average researcher even believes that this milestone will probably be reached within the next century-and-a-half. I’m unsure whether this particular estimate is reasonable. I do agree, though, that something like complete automation will probably become possible eventually. I expect human labor to lose nearly all of its value once it becomes cheaper and more effective to simply use machines to get things done.

If human labor loses its value, then this strikes me as bad news for democracy. It would seem to eliminate most of the incentive for elites to accept democratization. If the suppression of protests can be automated, using systems that are more effective than humans, then public revolt would become much less threatening. Striking and resisting conscription would also, obviously, become totally obsolete as a method of applying public pressure. Elites would have weaker incentives to make any concessions at all.

Furthermore, it seems to me, elites would have more to lose from democracy. In a world without work, the two central forms of income would be welfare payments and passive income from investments. We should not be surprised if there is a huge lower class that depends on welfare payments to survive. Demands for radical redistribution might then become more common, for a few reasons: income polarization would be higher, redistribution would be simpler and less disruptive, and wealth levels would become extremely transparently divorced from merit. More moderate forms of redistribution would also stop benefitting elites at all. The resources and freedoms of common people would simply have no connection to economic growth.

The Valley of Democracy

One perspective on our place in history is that we are living in the little valley between industrialization and widespread automation. This valley has just the right conditions for democracy to flourish. When we leave the valley, though, we will once again be entering territory where democracy can hardly grow at all.

Of course, maybe whatever economic changes are coming will be fine for democracy. No one can make confident predictions here. Still, if I had to bet, I would bet against democracy. If we put aside economic theories and simply note the extreme rareness of democracy, throughout nearly the entire history of states, then a major decline in democracy seems more likely than not. If we take economic theories into account, then the analysis becomes much murkier. To my mind, though, this analysis is not reassuring. We should mourn democracy if it dies, but we shouldn’t be surprised.

Here’s a longer podcast interview with Garfinkel where he goes into more details on his research.

A lot of techno-optimisim has come from living through a brief era where technological progress was unusually rapid and correlated with political liberalism. America beat the Soviet Union partly because it was massively more technologically dynamic. This was an unbelievable achievement driven by the exact attitudes and ways of working and thinking techno-optimists prize and push. But I don’t see why the relationship between technology and freedom is guaranteed indefinitely into the future. Democracy and liberalism depend on large coalitions of people being economically valuable to one another. If that’s significantly undermined by AI, the world could quickly become unfree.

The arrival of the technology of farming probably made life much worse for the average person. The ability to generate and store surplus food through agriculture facilitated the emergence of specialized roles, but also led to the concentration of wealth and power. Hierarchical social structures developed, with a ruling elite controlling resources and labor. This was a stark departure from the more egalitarian nature of hunter-gatherer bands.

Via the miracle of the Industrial Revolution, we eventually clawed our way out of the brutal stupid simple hierarchical societies farming imposed on us, 6000 years later. We obviously invented new terrifying forms of domination, but it seems like the average person’s life now is almost definitely better than it was 300 years ago. It’s worth noting though that the Industrial Revolution was a gigantic catastrophe for farmed animals, who are the vast majority of beings affected by it. The technology of farming seems to have locked in a brutal hierarchical world we only managed to escape from in the last few centuries. We’re pretty unclear about our current trajectory.

If you put me in 1960s America, I would be an intense techno-optimist. If you put me in 4000 BCE Mesopotamia, I would be an intense techno-pessimist and Luddite. Both have been reasonable at different times due to the nature of technological determinism. Simple techno-optimism or pessimism doesn’t make sense when you look at the full story of history. The question now is how people in the mid 2020s should react to the arrival of AI. While there’s a lot that I’m excited about, there’s enough reasons to worry that I want wariness about technology to receive deep respect in all conversations, and not just be sneered at like it’s a result of someone’s fear of the future or negative relationship to ambition and striving. These debates and ideas are too complex and important to be steamrolled by the culture war, by either side.

Some other good reading on technological determinism

Helen Toner recently had a great exploration of the rival values at play in debates about AI safety and progress here. I’d recommend reading the whole thing, it’s summarized in this quote:

These dichotomies—pro-tech vs. anti-tech, risk-embracing vs. risk-averse—are awkward fits for the arguments people want to have about AI safety ideas. In her book, Postrel sets out to describe a different dichotomy, one that in my view much better captures what it is about AI safety ideas that gets critics’ hackles up.

The Future and Its Enemies is a manifesto for what Postrel calls “dynamism—a world of constant creation, discovery, and competition.” Its antithesis is “stasis—a regulated, engineered world... [that values] stability and control.”

The great holy text of the uncertain technological determinist is Von Neumann’s Can We Survive Technology? I’d assign this as mandatory reading to everyone if I could. The closing passage summarizes how we should think about new technology well:

Present awful possibilities of nuclear warfare may give way to others even more awful. After global climate control becomes possible, perhaps all our present involvements will seem simple. We should not deceive ourselves: once such possibilities become actual, they will be exploited. It will, therefore, be necessary to develop suitable new political forms and procedures. All experience shows that even smaller technological changes than those now in the cards profoundly transform political and social relationships. Experience also shows that these transformations are not a priori predictable and that most contemporary "first guesses" concerning them are wrong. For all these reasons, one should take neither present difficulties nor presently proposed reforms too seriously.

The one solid fact is that the difficulties are due to an evolution that, while useful and constructive, is also dangerous. Can we produce the required adjustments with the necessary speed? The most hopeful answer is that the human species has been subjected to similar tests before and seems to have a congenital ability to come through, after varying amounts of trouble. To ask in advance for a complete recipe would be unreasonable. We can specify only the human qualities required: patience, flexibility, intelligence.

We don’t have much history of technology to work off

Some people very confidently dismiss concern about future AI systems because of the history of technology. A common point is that people used to be worried that electricity would destroy the world, and electricity was one of the most emancipatory technologies ever. Because people have worried about past technology, and it’s turned out to be fine, we can assume worry about new technology is irrational and wrong.

This way of talking is silly, because we don’t actually have many examples of new transformative technology to work off.

Here’s a list of general-purpose technologies and when they were invented, from Wikipedia:

12 of the 25 “general purpose technologies” humans have come up with have come in the last 200 years. Comparing this to the full 9000 year span of technology:

We’re living in a weird time.

It makes sense that most significant tech advances have only happened in the last 200 years, because the human population only very recently boomed, so we suddenly have a lot more people to work on inventing new technology:

If we redraw the timeline of humans using technology, where instead the timeline is just counting the total number of people born rather than the years that have passed, the chart looks much more reasonable:

The average person born after the Industrial Revolution seems to be about twice as good at coming up with new general purpose technology as the average person before the Industrial Revolution. This also makes sense, because the average person born after the Industrial Revolution is much richer than the average person before and has more control over their time and resources:

It seems ridiculous to extrapolate what future tech could be like based on the past. We’re in an incredibly weird era of human history where a crazy amount of new technology has (from the perspective of history) very suddenly flooded our lives. There are some examples of past technology, like electricity, where people thought electricity would be a much bigger problem than it was.

There are other examples, like nuclear weapons, where people could pretty easily predict that they would change the world. The World Set Free by HG Wells described in 1914 what a nuclear war might look like 30 years before the first atom bombs were invented. People were right to worry.

It remains to be seen how big of a deal machines that can mimic a lot of what happens in the human brain will be, but we can’t make super confident predictions about the next hundred years of AI progress based on the trajectory of past technology. Humans are, relatively speaking, still incredibly new to our technological era, and no one knows what’s going to happen. People were wrong to freak out about electricity, but right to freak out about nuclear weapons. Predicting the future is hard. Sneering at anyone concerned about a new general purpose technology because the technological past has been fine misunderstands how new humans are to all this, and also ignores that some technologies (like nuclear weapons, and agriculture) did in fact made life much more dangerous for the average person.

4: A final rant: AI discourse is full of tribal memes

One reason I’ve started posting more about AI is that a lot of the discourse has been hijacked by unthinking culture war slogans and reactions. There’s a pattern of talking about it that I want to push back on.

People speak in post hoc rationalizations

As you get older, you notice how many of the average person’s beliefs are surprisingly surface level.

One jarring pattern is how blatantly people invent new beliefs in the moment (which often contradict their old beliefs) to signal tribal loyalty. If you present a new idea to someone, you can sometimes see them take the idea, play with it in their head to detect whether it’s of their tribe or not (like they’re doing a wine tasting), decide that it’s good or bad based on their tribal identity, immediately come up with a post hoc rationalization for why they happen to believe exactly what signals belonging to their tribe, and suggest that this rationalization is actually a deeply held principle they’ve always had and could have articulated clearly before. It’s obvious that if you had asked them to articulate the same principle a minute ago independent of the new idea you presented, they couldn’t do it.

When this happens, there’s this mutual sense of lying and not caring about the truth, and a lack of mutual respect. Both people sense what’s happening, but accept it as the normal way to talk and think. There’s even sometimes an implication that to talk as if you’re actually interested in what’s true is a sign that you’re not “with it,” and bad at picking up on what’s actually going on in the social space. This way of talking always makes me feel kind of dead.

An example is talking to some people from conservative political tribes about animal welfare. If I say “I’m vegan, I think factory farming is a gigantic moral catastrophe and might be the main bad thing society is doing right now,” some conservatives run the same internal process I just described. They use their tribal detectors, scan what team I’m on and decide I’m not on theirs. My statement gets translated as: “I’m blue tribe, I hate farmers, I hate masculinity, I want to make you weak.” The content gets ignored. What matters is that I’m an adversary. It’s time to develop post hoc ideas.

In response, they say things like “Animals were made for us to eat,” or “American farmers treat animals great,” even if these clearly weren’t their prior beliefs. You can tell because if the context were different (say we were in a relaxed, non-ideological conversation and I asked, “How do you think we should treat animals?”) many of the same people would probably give more thoughtful answers. They might talk about stewardship, protecting the natural world, or how big factory farms are disconnected from traditional, community-based farming.

My question coming away from this is always “Why can’t we just put down the game and talk about what we actually think? If you would say completely different things in different circumstances, why not just always say what you would if you were speaking more directly and to try to reflect what you actually feel like you internally believe?” The actual answer is unfortunately probably that reasoning itself evolved as a tool to do tribal signaling, not to figure out complex truths. The desire to signal our tribal loyalties runs way deeper than almost all other drives. It’s like the original sin of reason: hardwired into us from birth and constantly steering us away from the light of truth. Still, we obviously have the capacity to figure out outstandingly complex and subtle truths about the way the world actually works. Believing actually true things does matter beyond just giving each other status. We’ve found ways to avoid just tribally signaling all the time. Why don’t we use them more?

The obvious answer is that straying from our tribe feels bad, so entertaining new ideas on their own to determine if they’re true often requires at least a little bravery, and a lot of people just aren’t willing to make that leap. A life where every conversation about any new idea is a tribal test just seems so depressing. I suspect but can’t prove that this is more common now because of social media.

Ways this shows up in AI discourse

A lot of people who are having a bad time with AI seem to be the people who experience every new idea and trend as a test to see which tribe you’re in. Using AI is a way of failing their tribal test. This could explain why so much of the current AI discourse is full of post hoc opinions about something based on perceived tribal loyalty rather than curiosity. Anyone who’s actually sat down to use a chatbot for something they’re trying to understand knows that the chatbot isn’t constantly hallucinating or lying, and isn’t “glorified auto-complete” in the sense that it’s just randomly spitting out words that might or might not be coherent. Anyone who’s tried to rigorously budget their energy use for the sake of the climate knows that a 3 watt-hour ChatGPT search is so unbelievably minuscule that worrying about it is like worrying about the energy a digital clock’s using. These obvious facts have been effectively hidden from large groups of people because of their media diet and sense of tribal loyalty.

Value inconsistencies around this are jarring. People who are generally anti-car are suddenly ignoring that AI driven cars are crashing way way less often than human drivers. People who believe that anyone can make art, that anything can be art, that we shouldn’t gate keep the experience of art or require people to jump through arbitrary hoops to access it are suddenly basically aesthetic conservatives when AI art appears; accusing it of being lowest common denominator slop in language I can’t imagine them ever using about any other medium. People who have identified as philosophical materialists and atheists are suddenly talking like there’s something ineffable and magical about the human mind that machines will never be able to replicate. People who will say that all property is theft and pirate a lot of what they consume are suddenly really worried about AI disrespecting IP rights. The list goes on. All of these strike me as simple “AI isn’t in our tribe, we need to attack it” invented principles that no one believed a few years ago.

All of this isn’t to say that there aren’t real concerns about everything mentioned, only that a lot of the specific arguments people are using don’t make sense.

Overexcitement about AI has contradictions as well. Hyper-techno-optimist accelerationists will go back and forth between arguing that AI is going to be an epochal world-changing technology to such an extent that America needs to get to it before everyone else to remake the world in its image, and also that there’s no way that AI could introduce any new catastrophic risks to the world and it’s ridiculous to assume it will be so powerful. This often feels much more like a way of saying “I want to be seen as a dynamic forward-looking freedom-loving Randian hero, and not be held down by luddites” than a serious engagement with the arguments for ways AI could become dangerous.

Different tribes have developed vast catalogs of common beliefs about AI that are mostly wrong. It’s understandable that a lot of people don’t understand the specifics of AI, but many go way beyond this to both accept and make new bold false claims about AI’s current abilities, energy use, and other problems with it that don’t make sense if you allow yourself to think about AI for a few minutes without using memorized slogans from social media. This podcast episode is a good example of a more or less nonstop stream of misleading or just incorrect claims about AI systems, with the background feel of saying “AI is not in our tribe. It’s a bad guy. By hating it together we’ll be on the same team. We won’t allow it to trick us.”

This is a big reason I’ve been drawn to post a lot more about AI recently. There’s a much more massive gulf between the capabilities of AI tools right now and the broader cultural conversation about them than any new tech I can remember. It’s like being around for the early days of the internet, only this time everyone is suddenly much more tribalistic about it and randomly hate it for confusing signaling reasons that don’t match reality or their prior beliefs. AI’s too interesting as a new piece of technology to just sit back and watch that happen. There are a lot of good reasons to be concerned about AI, but a lot of those reasons are rooted in the fact that AI as it exists right now is already incredibly powerful at what it’s being used for, and could get more powerful over time.

I don’t feel obligated to sell AI to people, but I’d really rather people not play these games of coming up with post hoc incorrect tribal ideas about something that’s going to be so important to the next decade. There’s an incredible amount of low hanging fruit in trying to help people ease out of their tribal thinking about this and just look more seriously at what’s happening.

To help people step outside of the fray of tribal thinking, it’s especially important to be kind, upbeat, firm, and show them that you understand their background concerns and aren’t trying to just score cheap points for a rival tribe. I think the best communication about AI happening right now checks all those boxes, and I’m trying to mimic that more on this blog. The theme of my last few posts have been trying to gently push back on inconsistent tribal beliefs about AI art, AI energy use, AI and people’s stated beliefs about philosophy of mind, and also how to learn more about AI in the first place, why people are so inconsistent in the first place, and how to try to be more open to new ideas. It’s been an especially fruitful topic. If you’re interested in AI comms at all it seems like having this background framework of “I’m trying to reveal a nuanced situation to you that’s closer to the truth beyond the buzzwords you’ve memorized” will go much farther than trying to engage directly in the culture war with your own buzzwords and tribal language.

AI is unlike most other culture war issues in that a lot of false claims about it can be disproven by just having people sit and play with a model for a bit and see for themselves what it’s like. Inviting more people to do this can be a fun role to play.
